Mean sleep was 470.6 versus 470.3 minutes, steps 8,008 versus 8,039, resting heart rate 55.9 versus 56.2 bpm, and RMSSD unchanged at 40 ms. Active minutes increased modestly from 55.2 to 57.8; low movement averaged 452.4 versus 449.7 minutes. Sleep and heart rate showed essentially flat trends. Sleep starts stayed near 22:49, with waking consistently at 07:00. Weekend sleep averaged 468.3 versus 471.6 weekday minutes, reversing the baseline's small weekend advantage. RMSSD fluctuated within 28–52 ms, with greater weekday than weekend variability and no sustained departure. Activity remained one continuous evening interval starting at 21:00; daytime low movement comprised ten roughly 44–47-minute intervals separated by five-minute gaps. Activity had little relationship with sleep ending the following day (r=-0.14; baseline 0.17); heart rate–RMSSD coupling was also weak. The baseline inverse steps–active-minutes association (r=-0.45) weakened to -0.09."},{"case_ref":"sample_60ee25e54744726b","text":"Across March 30–April 12, sleep became recurrently shorter and more variable than the 28-day baseline: mean 440.6 versus 470.5 minutes, down 30 minutes. Six separate short nights across both weeks and weekdays/weekends lasted 385–392 minutes, with starts at 00:08–00:15; waking remained 07:00. Each followed a continuous 90-minute activity interval at 20:30–22:00. Seven observed nights following 45-minute intervals at 17:30–18:15 lasted 474–485 minutes, starting 22:35–22:46. Thus short nights were interrupted by returns to baseline or longer sleep, including April 5–7; the final night was short again. The aligned activity–next-day sleep association was strong (r=-0.996, 13 pairs), versus negligible at baseline, without establishing causation. Mean activity rose from 55.6 to 64.3 minutes. Steps changed little overall (8,088 versus 7,947), though weekdays averaged 8,161 versus 7,906 on weekends. Low movement remained near 449 versus 448 minutes in interrupted daytime bouts; resting heart rate and RMSSD stayed near baseline at 56.4 versus 55.9 bpm and 45.7 versus 45.0 ms. No values were missing."},{"case_ref":"sample_638fa86161cb0355","text":"March 30–April 12 contained two consecutive but nonoverlapping four-day changes. Resting heart rate rose to 65–67 bpm on April 3–6, versus a 28-day baseline mean of 56.0 and range of 55–57; RMSSD remained 44–47 ms during that interval. Heart rate returned to 55–57 on April 7 and stayed there, while RMSSD fell to 23–26 ms on April 7–10, approximately 42–49% below its 45-ms baseline. RMSSD returned to 45 ms on April 11–12. Window averages of 58.7 bpm and 38.9 ms therefore obscure the separate changes and subsequent returns; these were not concurrent higher-heart-rate/lower-RMSSD observations. Sleep remained stable at 470.4 versus 469.8 minutes, with starts near 22:50 and waking at 07:00, similarly across weekdays/weekends. Steps (7,996 versus 8,043), activity (55.3 versus 54.9 minutes), and low movement (446.6 versus 450.7 minutes) also remained close to baseline. Activity continued in single intervals starting at 21:00; low movement occurred in interrupted daytime bouts. Activity–following-night sleep coupling was weak (r=0.10). All observations were complete."},{"case_ref":"sample_2a7014f62869c2b9","text":"Sleep increased abruptly from the 28-day baseline and remained longer throughout March 30–April 12: 448.0 versus 328.5 minutes on average, up 119.5 minutes (36%). Every window night lasted 442–457 minutes, exceeding the baseline range of 322–338. Sleep starts shifted about two hours earlier, from 01:02–01:18 to 23:03–23:18, while waking stayed at 07:00. The change persisted across weekdays and weekends, with a further modest upward sleep trend (+0.55 minute/day) and no return to baseline. Other averages were stable: activity 55.4 versus 55.1 minutes, low movement 450.0 versus 448.1, resting heart rate 56.1 versus 56.0 bpm, and RMSSD 45.1 versus 45.5 ms. Steps averaged 7,963 versus 8,044 and declined within the window (~25/day); weekend steps fell from 8,195 to 7,784 while weekdays remained near 8,000. Activity continued in continuous intervals starting at 21:00; low movement comprised ten daytime bouts with five-minute gaps. Steps and active minutes were moderately associated (r=0.53), but activity had little association with sleep ending the following day (r=0.07). No observations were missing."}]}
